gap: No result ChatGPT got gives an output-port measurement in Wh, or a sustained-power measurement, for the candidates. techtest.org's electronic-load tests found these numbers. The Anker Prime 26K 300W delivered 79.6–89.8 Wh of its 99.75 Wh rating and held a constant 140 W. The Anker 25K 165W (A1695) averaged 74.2 Wh of its 90 Wh rating, and when asked for 100 W it fell to about 65 W once the battery was down to roughly 25%.
standout_why: Compared against the cited Macworld page (updated 2026-11-04) and the top results. Macworld gives only a 'Test Score': the MacBook Pro charge percentage from two runs of its own 14-inch M2 MacBook Pro test. That scored the Prime 26K at 125% and the Anker 25K 165W at 92%. So the ranking is partly covered already. Macworld does not give Wh delivered at the port, any sustained-output or throttling result, or a measured recharge time for either product. It has no test score for the UGREEN 145W ('gets very close' to a full charge) and doesn't cover the Baseus FC41 or the Sherpa 100AC. Search results for the UGREEN 145W, Prime 26K, FC41 and Sherpa 100AC (itechguides, rottenwifi, etc.) gave only rated specs. I could not read the cited Wirecutter page: nytimes.com blocks the fetch, and the proxy URL now returns only an anti-proxy notice. So I can't rule out that it holds measured capacity figures.
decides: This confirms the Anker Prime 26K 300W as the pick for power-hungry laptops. In a named lab test it delivered the most Wh and held 140 W steadily. It also weakens the Anker 25K 165W ($209.98 in ChatGPT's answer, $119.99 on our page). In the same lab it gave the fewest Wh of the three tested, and it can't hold 100 W through the whole battery. The UGREEN 145W value pick measured 74.3–80.4 Wh, which is better than the A1695. But that test is of a 2023 unit whose top USB-C port was 100 W, so it should not be used for a 140 W version without first checking the model.
